title: Andrew Ross Sorkin on the Crash of 1929 & The Parallels We See Today | The Real Eisman Playbook

metadata.title: Andrew Ross Sorkin on the Crash of 1929 & The Parallels We See Today | The Real Eisman Playbook

summary: Andrew Ross Sorkin discusses the human incentives and policy failures surrounding 1929. Eisman emphasizes leverage, shared institutional exposures, short-selling survival and the danger of assuming officials already understand a crisis. This is mainly historical explanation, not a prediction of another crash. Original Fed records contradict the guest's assertion that policymakers could not contemplate rate increases in 1929, and preexisting bank capital rules qualify the repeated no-rules narrative.
assessment: Claims are assessed individually. Empirical premises are not treated as successful forecasts. Unverified magnitudes and causal stories remain unresolved; subjective investment judgments are not assigned directional wins.
speaker_map_notes: Steve Eisman interviews Andrew Ross Sorkin. Historical explanations by the guest are kept separate from Eisman's crisis framework and retrospective process revision.
framework_points: Map leverage, shared assets and funding links before calling a downturn systemic.
Separate correct bearish direction from the ability to survive a short.
Do not assume policymakers possess all available information or can act promptly.
Distinguish the crash, the ensuing depression, the start of recovery and full employment.
Use historical analogies as risk prompts rather than deterministic forecasts.
Check original policy actions before inferring motives from a narrative.
tools_and_charts: Bank capital and reserve rules before modern ratios
Layered leverage in old trusts and modern vehicles
transcript_cautions: Biographical trivia and speculative mental-health characterization are omitted as immaterial to the investment audit.
Eisman's initial unemployment number is immediately corrected and accepted, so it is not a separate forecast error.
Book anecdotes remain unresolved where the underlying archives were not inspected.
Sorkin explicitly says he is not forecasting another 1929.

evidence.title: Portfolio Margin FAQ
evidence.finding: Portfolio margin is a risk-based alternative to conventional strategy-based margin, with separate eligibility and computation requirements. A two-to-one initial-stock-margin example is not a universal leverage ceiling.

assumptions: An asset position is financed with debt fixed in nominal amount.
Equity is the residual asset value less debt.
evidence_basis.proof: With equity equal to one tenth of assets, a 10% asset-price decline erases initial equity before interest and transaction costs. A small margin deposit therefore magnifies both gains and losses.

claims.claim: There were no genuine regulatory bank-capital requirements before the crash.
claims.speaker: Andrew Ross Sorkin
claims.test: Inspect the relevant original financial, operational or economic data and compare the claimed mechanism with competing explanations.
claims.reason: Minimum charter capital and reserve rules already existed. Absence of modern capital-to-asset ratios is not absence of regulatory capital requirements.

evidence.title: National Banking Acts of 1863 and 1864
evidence.finding: National bank rules included minimum capital levels and reserve requirements based on the city's population and designation. These were not modern risk-weighted ratios, but banking was not without capital rules.

assumptions: A short position faces interim mark-to-market losses, margin limits, borrow costs or recall risk.
Prices can rise before a later decline.
evidence_basis.proof: An investor forced to close during an interim rise realizes a loss and cannot benefit from the subsequent fall. Forecast direction alone therefore does not guarantee a profitable executable trade.

claims.speaker: Andrew Ross Sorkin
claims.test: Inspect the relevant original financial, operational or economic data and compare the claimed mechanism with competing explanations.
claims.reason: Leverage is an amplifier, but the broad claim that every major crash requires it is not established. Unlevered assets can reprice sharply when expected cash flows or discount rates change.

assumptions: Leveraged institutions have capital small relative to exposed assets.
Several important institutions share exposure and have interconnected funding obligations.
evidence_basis.proof: Common asset losses erode capital; forced deleveraging depresses asset prices further and unmet funding obligations spread stress. Derivative exposures can add contingent obligations to this mechanism.

claims.claim: The October 1929 crash was followed by years of bank failures, trade disruption and unemployment rather than being a one-day event that ended the crisis.
claims.speaker: Andrew Ross Sorkin
claims.test: Inspect the relevant original financial, operational or economic data and compare the claimed mechanism with competing explanations.
claims.reason: The extended contraction is supported. Listing abandonment of gold among adverse dominoes obscures evidence that leaving gold aided recovery; precise failure and unemployment counts were not independently reconciled.

evidence.title: Money, Gold, and the Great Depression
evidence.finding: Analysis describes monetary contraction, bank failures and gold-standard constraints. Leaving gold and stabilizing banks enabled strong growth from 1933 to 1937; recovery began well before wartime full employment.

evidence.title: Federal Reserve Board annual report 1929
evidence.finding: Contemporaneous report records the New York discount-rate increase from 5% to 6% effective August 9, intended to restrain speculation. This contradicts the claim policymakers could not contemplate raising rates in 1929.
